title: Buddhaghosa arrives
hookLine: the scholar comes to Sri Lanka and writes the great commentaries in Pali
last: MADE FOR THE SERENE JOY OF THE FAITHFUL.

cards: Tangled within, tangled without, and people everywhere caught in the knots. Who can work them loose? In a short sutta, a question like that is put to the Buddha, and he answers in a single verse.
Much later, a scholar from India built an entire book on that one verse.
The chronicle remembers him as Buddhaghosa, and says he crossed to Sri Lanka to study the old commentaries kept at the Great Monastery in Anuradhapura.

teach.b: First, why he came. The later part of the chronicle says Buddhaghosa was a learned man in India who heard that the commentaries on the Buddha's discourses were kept in Sri Lanka, in the Sinhala language.
So he went to study them at the Great Monastery, the Mahavihara.
Second, the test. The elders, the story says, didn't simply hand over their library. They gave him verses and asked him to show what he could do.
At the heart of his answer is the Buddha's reply to the tangle: a wise person, established in virtue, developing mind and understanding, can untangle the tangle.
His answer became the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification: a long, careful map of virtue, concentration and wisdom, all hung on that one verse. Third, the legend.
The story says the gods hid his finished book, and he wrote it again; they hid it once more, and he wrote it a third time.
Read side by side, the copies agreed word for word. Some readers take that as a miracle. Others read it as the tradition's way of saying this work can be trusted.
Tradition credits him with rendering the Sinhala commentaries into Pali, the language of the texts, so monks anywhere could read them.
Theravada teachers still turn to those commentaries to explain what a word in a sutta means. When a monk somewhere explains a difficult line, Buddhaghosa may well be in the room.

how: Theravada monks study the Visuddhimagga and the Pali commentaries alongside the suttas, and teachers draw on them to explain the meaning of words and passages in the canon.

games.q: you're a visiting scholar. the elders give you verses to explain before they'll open their library. what do you do?
o: give a short talk on them.
write a whole book on the path from one verse.
refuse: your learning speaks for itself.
games.why: the chronicle says his answer was the Visuddhimagga, a full map of virtue, concentration and wisdom built on the verse about the tangle.

practice: Take today's verse in plain words: established in virtue, developing mind and understanding, one can untangle the tangle.
Hold one piece at a time for a few breaths, steady footing, the mind as it is right now, one tangle you'd like to see clearly, without hurrying to answers.
